'''''Erigeron sumatrensis''''' (syn. ''Conyza sumatrensis'') is an annual [[herb]] probably native to [[South America]], but widely [[naturalised]] in tropical and subtropical regions, and regarded as an invasive weed in many places.{{r|powo|fna}}<ref>[https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/11159722#page/98/mode/1up Pruski, J.F. & G. Sancho. 2006. ''Conyza sumatrensis'' var. ''leiotheca'' (Compositae: Astereae), a new combination for a common neotropical weed. Novon 16(1): 96–101]</ref>It is a perennial in the Western Cape of South Africa.

In the British Isles it is known as '''Guernsey fleabane'''.<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007|accessdate=2014-10-17}}</ref> Other common names include '''fleabane''', '''tall fleabane''', '''broad-leaved fleabane''', '''white horseweed''', and '''Sumatran fleabane'''.{{cn|date=August 2020}}

==Description==
When fully grown (in summer or autumn), ''Erigeron sumatrensis'' reaches {{Convert|1 to 2|m|ft}} in height. Flowers are white rather than purple-pink. Its leaves are like dandelion leaves, but longer, thinner and more like primrose leaves in colour and texture. Its seeding heads are like dandelions, but straw coloured and smaller.<ref>See pictures at [http://www.iewf.org/weedid/Conyza_sumatrensis.htm International Environmental Weed Foundation]</ref> In certain countries the plant has started to exhibit resistance to herbicides.<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20020420153136/http://www.weedscience.org/Case/Case.asp?ResistID=126 Sumatran Fleabane], Weedscience.org</ref>

==Distribution==
It probably originates from South America, but is now naturalised in North America, Europe,<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.kuleuven-kortrijk.be/bioweb/?lang=en&detail=732&titel=Sumatran%20fleabane%20-%20Conyza%20sumatrensis |title=Fleabane in Holland |access-date=2008-03-01 |archive-date=2011-10-03 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111003094715/http://www.kuleuven-kortrijk.be/bioweb/?lang=en&detail=732&titel=Sumatran%20fleabane%20-%20Conyza%20sumatrensis |url-status=dead }}</ref> Africa,<ref>[https://www.zimbabweflora.co.zw/speciesdata/species.php?species_id=159010  Flora of Zimbabwe: ''Conyza sumatrensis'']</ref> Asia,<ref>[https://www.botanic.jp/plants-aa/ooaret.htm Sumatran Fleabane in Japan]</ref> and Australasia.<ref>[http://www.hear.org/pier/species/conyza_sumatrensis.htm Pacific Island Ecosystems at Risk (PIER): ''Conyza sumatrensis'']</ref> It poses a significant threat to wildlife conservation areas and other reserves. In Britain, of the non-native former ''Conyza'' species, it is the second most abundant (after ''[[Erigeron canadensis]]'') and is typically found in London and the South East of England. It was first recorded in London by Brian Wurzell in 1984,<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://freespace.virgin.net/conserving.bevan/talk2.htm |title=Fleabane in London |access-date=2008-03-01 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110604111307/http://freespace.virgin.net/conserving.bevan/talk2.htm |archive-date=2011-06-04 |url-status=dead }}</ref>
and noted in France at [[Saint-Sozy]] (Dordogne) in 2006.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.naturetrek.co.uk/reports/France%20-%20The%20Dordogne%20-%20tour%20report%20(May%2006).pdf |title=France – The Dordogne |accessdate=2011-10-18 |author=Mark Galliott |date=June 2006 |work=Tour Report |publisher=Naturetrek Wildlife Holidays |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20070929015715/http://www.naturetrek.co.uk/reports/France%20-%20The%20Dordogne%20-%20tour%20report%20%28May%2006%29.pdf |archivedate=2007-09-29 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

==Taxonomic note==
Older literature such as Flora of Turkey may quote ''Conyza albida'' Willd. ex Spreng. intending what is now ''E. sumatrensis'' Retz., and should be taken as such; likewise other literature references may do so; the type has subsequently been revised and ''Conyza albida'' Willd. ex Spreng. is now viewed as a synonym for ''Erigeron floribundus'' (Kunth) Sch.Bip. <ref name="albida">[https://www.phytoneuron.net/2018Phytoneuron/27PhytoN-Conyzasumatrensis.pdf ''Erigeron Floribundus'' and ''E. Sumatrensis'' (Asteraceae) In The USA And Mexico, 2018 by Guy L. Nesom], p16 in section on ''Erigeron floribundus''</ref>
